race.office: Governor of Arizona (joint ticket with lieutenant governor, first time under Prop. 131)

nominee.t: Democratic nominee, unopposed in the July 21, 2026 primary. Running mate: former Mesa Mayor John Giles (mayor 2014–2025), a longtime Republican who changed his registration to independent on May 17 (2026, per context) and voted in the Democratic primary; announced Aug 11, 2026.

ballot.t: General ballot: Hobbs/Giles (D), Andy Biggs/Sine Kerr (R), Risa Lombardo (G; disavowed by the state Green Party), Teri Ann Hourihan (No Labels). See az-races.json for the verified ballot.

oneliner.t: Democratic governor of Arizona since January 2023, a former social worker, state legislator (2011–2019) and Secretary of State (2019–2023), seeking a second term with independent John Giles as her running mate.

hometown.t: Tempe, Arizona (grew up there; Seton Catholic High School, 1988)

upbringing.t: Kathleen Marie Hobbs was born in Phoenix and grew up in Tempe in a middle-class family with a twin sister, Becky; at times the family relied on food stamps and, in her own account, on its church community. She graduated from Seton Catholic High School (1988), earned a bachelor's in social work at Northern Arizona University (1992) and a master's in social work at Arizona State University (1995), and worked as a social worker, including as chief compliance officer at the Sojourner Center domestic-violence shelter. She married Patrick Goodman in 1996; they have two children. She is Catholic.

career.role: Social worker; chief compliance officer, Sojourner Center (domestic-violence shelter); adjunct professor at Paradise Valley Community College and ASU

platform.t: Campaigns on bringing down prices; touts middle-class tax cuts, a senior deduction, no state tax on tips and overtime, repeal of the tax on rent, and down-payment help for first-time buyers.
Touts erasing medical debt and lowering prescription-drug costs.
Cites ending state-land leases of Saudi-owned Fondomonte, which farms with Arizona groundwater and ships crops overseas.
Cites sending the National Guard to the border and funding local law enforcement for border security and anti-trafficking work.
Says she will keep working to fix the education system; as governor proposed rolling back the universal ESA expansion (2023) and later an ESA accountability plan (2024).

promises.t: Keep bringing down costs for families, fix the state's education system and keep Arizona safe (stated reelection focus).

claims.claim: Grew up in a working-class Tempe family that at times relied on its church community and food stamps.

said.where: 2026 primary candidate statement, Clean Elections voter guide (campaign site not reachable)

record.t: Wikipedia's biography, citing earlier reporting, says she grew up in Tempe in a middle-class family that sometimes relied on food stamps. 'Working-class' vs. 'middle-class' is characterization.

claims.claim: Worked her way through college at NAU and ASU and became a social worker.

said.where: 2026 primary candidate statement, Clean Elections voter guide

record.t: B.S.W., Northern Arizona University (1992); M.S.W., Arizona State University (1995); career as a social worker. Whether she worked through school was not independently checked.

claims.claim: Helped lead one of the largest domestic violence shelters in the country.

said.where: 2026 primary candidate statement, Clean Elections voter guide

record.t: Her role as chief compliance officer at the Sojourner Center is documented; the shelter's national size ranking was not checked.

claims.claim: Championed middle-class tax cuts that save 88% of Arizonans money, plus a $6,000 senior deduction and elimination of taxes on tips and overtime.

said.where: 2026 primary candidate statement, Clean Elections voter guide

record.t: The deductions are now law: the $18.3B budget she signed in June 2026 adopted full conformity with the 2025 federal tax law, including no state tax on tips and overtime from July 1 and a senior credit. Earlier she had vetoed two Republican bills containing the same deductions because they also carried corporate breaks, and issued a November 2025 executive order mirroring the individual deductions before they were law. She accepted full conformity in negotiations. The 88% figure was not checked.

claims.claim: Cancelled $642 million in medical debt for almost half a million Arizonans.

said.where: 2026 primary candidate statement, Clean Elections voter guide

record.t: As of Dec 22, 2025, the program had erased $642 million in medical debt for more than 485,000 Arizonans. The state used federal American Rescue Plan money ($30 million, per Wikipedia) to pay the nonprofit Undue Medical Debt, which buys debt for pennies on the dollar and forgives it.

claims.claim: Canceled leases held by a Saudi Arabian corporation that pumps Arizona groundwater and ships crops overseas.

said.where: 2026 primary candidate statement, Clean Elections voter guide; also 2025 launch video

record.t: On Oct 2, 2023 the State Land Department terminated one of Fondomonte Arizona's four Butler Valley leases and said it would not renew the other three when they expired in February 2024. The stated legal basis was an uncured lease default (missing fuel-storage containment), not water use. The leases did end; the framing omits the stated reason.

claims.claim: Delivered over $215 million to local law enforcement for border security and anti-trafficking work.

said.where: 2026 primary candidate statement, Clean Elections voter guide

record.t: No budget or grant record for the total was retrieved.

claims.claim: Her efforts led to the seizure of 12 million fentanyl pills and nearly 5,000 pounds of meth.

said.where: 2026 primary candidate statement, Clean Elections voter guide

record.t: No task-force seizure data was retrieved.

claims.claim: Cut prescription drug costs by up to 80%.

said.where: 2026 primary candidate statement, Clean Elections voter guide

record.t: The program behind the figure was not identified or checked.

said.t: As a 2022 candidate said border security is a federal responsibility and the state's role should be limited, while border communities get the money and law-enforcement resources they need.

did.t: Ordered the Arizona National Guard to the border (Dec 17, 2023) and now campaigns on the deployment and on funding local law enforcement for border work. She vetoed SB 1164 (2025), which would have required state and local cooperation with federal immigration detainers.

promises_prev.promise: Repeal Arizona's pre-Roe near-total abortion ban, through the Legislature first or a 2024 ballot measure

evidence.t: Signed the repeal of the 1864 ban on May 2, 2024; it took effect Sept 14, 2024. Voters then passed Proposition 139 (2024), protecting abortion up to fetal viability.

complicating.t: The repeal needed votes from a few Republican legislators in a GOP-controlled Legislature. The constitutional protection came from a citizen initiative, not from her.

promises_prev.promise: Roll back the 2022 universal expansion of the Empowerment Scholarship Account (voucher) program

evidence.t: Her 2023 executive budget and first State of the State called for rolling back the expansion, which she said could cost $1.5B over a decade. In January 2024 she shifted to an eight-point accountability plan (background checks, manual approval of purchases over $500) instead of repeal. Superintendent Tom Horne said she had shifted her view.

complicating.t: Republicans control the Legislature, which must pass any change. Enrollment had reached about 73,000–74,000 students by January 2024. Whether later budgets changed ESA rules was not checked.

promises_prev.promise: Create an annual $250-per-child tax credit for families earning $100,000 or less

evidence.t: The June 2026 budget she signed includes an expanded child tax credit starting the following year. Its amount and income limits were not checked against her 2022 terms.

complicating.t: The credit came as part of full federal tax conformity negotiated with Republicans, not as her standalone proposal.

entries.t: Pledged to roll back the universal expansion.
Executive budget and State of the State called for rollback; said it would 'likely bankrupt the state.'
Proposed an accountability and transparency plan instead of repeal.
Vetoed two GOP conformity bills over corporate provisions; issued a November 2025 executive order mirroring the individual deductions.
Accepted full conformity in the bipartisan $18.3B budget, including $1.4B in tax cuts over several years.
Halted executions on taking office and commissioned a review.
Ended the review; executions resumed (Mar 19, 2025; Oct 17, 2025; May 20, 2026).
Border security is primarily a federal job.
Deployed the National Guard to the border.

statements.t: Vetoed HB 2867, which would have let people sue teachers and professors personally over antisemitic teaching or conduct and put the IHRA definition of antisemitism into state law. She said the bill was an attack on teachers rather than about antisemitism, called antisemitism 'a scourge,' and noted she had signed expanded Holocaust-education requirements the year before plus $7 million for Phoenix's first permanent Holocaust education center.

fec.source: State data — Arizona campaign-finance filings as reported by news outlets (seethemoney.az.gov could not be opened). Not FEC data.
fec.src_note: Cycle receipts of $9.5M are KTAR's figure. Disbursements are 'more than $11 million' total, $7.4M of it in Q2 (KJZZ). Sources conflict: the Arizona Mirror and the campaign put Q2 raised at about $2.6M and end-of-June cash at nearly $2.4M, while KTAR reported $1.7M raised in 'the spring' and about $1.4M on hand heading into the primary. Q2 cash fell from more than $7.1M to about $2.4M (Mirror). The campaign says most money came in contributions under $100. No named donors were reported. By Sept 8, AZ Family reported she had spent more than $10M on TV ads.

support: Democratic Governors Association — $10M pledged Jul 28, 2026 ('an initial deposit'); spending vehicle not named
oppose: Turning Point PAC — paid Sen. Jake Hoffman's firm 1Ten LLC about $1.5M to help defeat Hobbs and elect Biggs (Axios); also spent $458,000 for Biggs before the primary (KJZZ)

fec.outside_note: The RGA had not committed money as of Jul 28 (it booked $10.2M by March in 2022). No FEC or state independent-expenditure totals were retrieved. The DGA's and Turning Point PAC's funders were not retrieved.

money2.note: No named donors in coverage read. DGA and Turning Point PAC funders not retrieved.

corp.t: Sunshine Residential Homes, a group-home company that is a state contractor, plus its founder Simon Kottoor and related people, gave $580,840 between Sept 2022 and May 2024 to the Arizona Democratic Party, her campaign, her inaugural fund and her legal defense fund (figure from her attorneys, per KJZZ). Earlier Arizona Republic reporting (via Axios) cited $400,000 to the inaugural fund and state party plus $150,000 to the legal defense fund. The Department of Child Safety later raised the company's rates. The Attorney General found no evidence of a pay-to-play scheme and brought no charges (Aug 21, 2026). The donations are documented; no causal link was found.

note.t: Her Arizona financial disclosure statement (filed with the Secretary of State) was not retrieved, so net worth and holdings are not recorded.

effectiveness.note: As governor she set a single-session veto record (63 vetoes by Apr 18, 2023; more than 100 by May 19, 2023). The Biggs campaign cites 541 total vetoes, which was not verified.

democracy.t: As Secretary of State during 2020, said her office ran 'the safest and most secure election in our state's history.'
As Secretary of State, wrote a letter criticizing the Senate-funded 2021 Maricopa County ballot review for lacking chain of custody. She received death threats and state police protection.
Her 2022 opponent, Kari Lake, did not concede and sued. The Arizona Supreme Court declined review in March 2023 and again in May 2023 after a trial. Hobbs was the winner, not the challenger.

debates.note: Declined the Oct 6, 2026 Clean Elections debate, as she declined to debate in 2022.

note.t: Born in Phoenix (1969), raised in Tempe, educated at NAU and ASU, and has lived and worked in Arizona since.

checks.legal: CourtListener and Justia were not reached; the URLs are outside this tool's provenance set. News and Wikipedia were searched for criminal or civil matters. Found: the Talonya Adams discrimination verdict (2021) and the Sunshine Residential pay-to-play investigation (closed by the AG on Aug 21, 2026 with no charges; the Auditor General review and a Senate special-counsel probe continue).
checks.foreign: FARA was not searched. No foreign-government or foreign-business ties surfaced in news reviewed. Russia banned her from entry in May 2023, which is a sanction by Russia, not a tie.
checks.claims: Mechanical sample: the campaign site (katiehobbs.org) could not be opened, so I used her own published 2026 candidate statement in the Clean Elections primary voter guide, every checkable item in order: food stamps/Tempe, NAU/ASU, shelter, tax cuts/88%/tips/overtime/senior deduction, rent tax (not rated: not checked), $642M medical debt, prescription costs, Fondomonte, $215M police, seizures. The top two ads by spending are unknown (more than $10M on TV), and no ad scripts were found.
checks.democracy: No congressional certification votes apply (never in Congress). Searched her 2020-era Secretary of State record and statements via Wikipedia and her 2022 Clean Elections statement. Her Nov 2020 certification act itself was not retrieved from a primary record. No statement on 2024 results was found.

legal.t: Talonya Adams, a Senate Democratic staffer fired in 2015 after raising race and gender pay concerns, sued the Arizona Senate. A 2019 jury awarded her $1M and reinstatement; after a retrial, a jury awarded $2.75M in November 2021, which reporting said was likely to be reduced to about $300,000 under the federal damages cap. Hobbs, then Senate minority leader, took part in the firing decision and testified at both trials but was not a defendant.
legal.short: Senate staffer verdict (Hobbs not a party)
legal.status: Jury verdict against the Arizona Senate, Nov 2021; final judgment amount not confirmed

legal.t: The Attorney General's office investigated for about two years whether rate increases for Sunshine Residential followed its donations. It found no evidence of a pay-to-play scheme and declined charges. It also found Hobbs did not advocate for the increase and was told only after DCS approved it, though she was never interviewed. Separately, the Legislature tasked the Auditor General with reviewing the contract, and Senate Republicans hired former Justice Andrew Gould as special counsel after issuing subpoenas.
legal.short: AG pay-to-play probe closed, no charges
legal.status: Criminal probe closed, no charges; legislative/Auditor General reviews ongoing as of Sep 2026

recordx.note: No missed-vote figure applies (executive). Arizona financial-disclosure timeliness and state campaign-finance compliance were not checked, so no recordx fields can be filled from primary records.

research_notes: MONEY: seethemoney.az.gov and azsos.gov could not be opened (provenance block), so all state figures come from news reports of her filings. KTAR and the Arizona Mirror disagree on Q2 receipts ($1.7M vs. $2.6M) and end-of-June cash (~$1.4M vs. ~$2.4M); fec.coh uses the Mirror/campaign figure. Resolve on SeeTheMoney. The pre-general report (covering July–early October) was not yet reported. Earlier cycles (2022 governor, 2018 SoS, legislative races) were not pulled. PROMISES: three 2022 promises scored. Others from Axios's 2022 list ($14,000 teacher raise, universal preschool, end the busing program, same-day registration, diaper/formula sales-tax exemption) were not checked; a human should complete them. CLAIMS: the campaign site was unreachable and her TV-ad scripts weren't found. Rated 5 checkable claims (3 true, 2 partly) plus 4 unverifiable. TALONYA ADAMS: confirm the named defendant before publication. SUNSHINE: donations are documented; the AG found no quid pro quo. Do not imply causation. The Auditor General and Senate (Gould) reviews were ongoing at last report. RUNNING MATE: Giles's record is his own and is not scored here. Photo not added.
